title: Nearly one in three homes was rented
description: Each square is about 1% of Australia’s 9.3 million occupied homes in 2021. Renters (31%) now almost match people who own outright (31%).

title: The separate house still defines the landscape
description: Box area shows how many occupied homes of each type there were. Seven in ten Australian homes are separate houses. Caravans, cabins and other homes (under 1%) are left out.

title: Apartments have a different tenure mix
description: Each column is a dwelling type, as wide as its share of homes; colours show how those homes are held. 63% of apartments are rented, against 21% of houses. Other and unstated dwelling types (1% of homes) are left out.

title: One in four people living alone has an apartment
description: Each band links a type of household to the kind of home it lives in; wider bands mean more households. Four in five families live in a separate house, but one in four people living alone has an apartment.

title: A national median hides local differences
description: Darker regions have higher median weekly rents. Manly in Sydney ($720) costs nine times as much as Arnhem Land in the NT ($80). The city maps are enlarged, so use their 10 km bars to judge distance. Outlines mark the three communities in chapter 3.

title: Rented homes crowd into the capital cities
description: Each dot is 1,000 rented homes, placed inside the small Census areas where those renters live. Most dots crowd into the capital cities and the coast. Zoom with the buttons, ctrl + scroll or double-click; drag to move.

title: Most regions charge between $300 and $450
description: Each bar counts the regions whose median weekly rent falls in a $50 band. 194 of 335 regions sit between $300 and $449 a week.

title: Higher-income places often have higher rents
description: Each dot is a region; dashed lines mark the Australian medians. Melbourne City renters pay above-median rent on below-median incomes.

title: There is no single rental market within a state
description: Each row is one state: the line runs from its cheapest region to its dearest, the box holds the middle half of its regions and the white mark is the typical region. NSW alone stretches from $150 to $720 a week.

title: Similar rents can come with very different homes
description: Each line is a region, read across four measures. Melbourne City and Casey – South charge almost the same rent, but 86% of Melbourne City’s homes are apartments, against 1% in Casey – South.

title: Rents are rising faster than prices overall
description: By July 2026 rents had risen 9.8% since April 2024, against 6.9% for prices across the economy, measured in the eight capital cities.

title: 263,800 assistance recipients still pay over half their income in rent
description: Circle area shows how many rent-assistance recipients pay more than half their income in rent after assistance; colour shows their share of the state’s recipients. NSW has the most, but the ACT has the highest share.

title: Students and job seekers face the most pressure
description: Each cell is the share of recipients in rental stress after assistance, by state and main payment. Students and apprentices on Youth Allowance top every state, at 74–87%.

title: Assistance helps, but 44% are still in rental stress
description: Each pair is the same recipients in March 2026: grey leaves rent assistance out, purple counts it. Rental stress means paying more than 30% of income in rent.
